title: De Eutychiana Haeresi Et Historia Libri Duo
author: Leo the Great

passages.original: Cyrilli doctrinam, se recipere fatebatur, addito tandem anathemate contra Manichæum, Valentinum, Apolli- narium, et Nestorium, omnesque hæreticos usque ad Simonem Magum, et eos qui dicunt carnem Domilli, et Dei nostri Jesu Christi de cælo descendisse (c) Narrat post hæc quemadmodum Eusebius Dorylæi eum, a sua pace extarbare volens, tamquam hæreticum in synodo Constantinopolitana sub Flaviano pustu ave- rit, nullam speciem hæreseoз libellis inserendo.Quare subjicit, episcopo Constantinopolitano præcipiente coactum fuisse ad satisfactionem accusationis.
passages.english: He declared that he accepted the teaching of Cyril, adding at last an anathema against Mani, Valentinus, Apollinaris and Nestorius, and all heretics back to Simon Magus, and against those who say that the flesh of our Lord and God Jesus Christ came down from heaven. After this he relates how Eusebius of Dorylaeum, wishing to drive him out of his peace, had accused him as a heretic in the synod of Constantinople under Flavian, without inserting any specific form of heresy in his written charges. Therefore he adds that, at the order of the bishop of Constantinople, he had been compelled to answer the accusation.
passages.notes: "(c)" is an editorial or footnote mark and has been omitted. "Domilli" read as "Domini"; "extarbare" as "exturbare"; "pustu averit" as "postulaverit" (accused); "hæreseoз" as "hæreseos". "Manichæum" is rendered as Mani, the founder of the Manichaeans. "Ad satisfactionem accusationis" is uncertain; it probably means "to answer the accusation".

passages.original: Nihilominus tamen, cum eorum judicia rescissa atque abolita a Julio et Romana synodo audierunt, minime attendentes quod omnium cura ad Roma- num spectal pontificem. ut ait Sozomenus, vel quod Romana Ecclesia privilegium habet prœ cœteris, ut scribit Socrates, Eusebiani graviter commoti conve- nerunt denuo Antiochiœ in unum, et epistolam verbis elegantibus ornatam ad Julium scribunt, eamque ple- nam ironiœ, et injuriarum non expertem gravissimarum. Hanc Eusebianorum commotionem idem Sozomenus narrat.
passages.english: Nevertheless, when they heard that their judgments had been rescinded and annulled by Julius and the Roman synod, paying no heed to the fact that the care of all belongs to the Roman pontiff, as Sozomen says, or that the Roman Church has a privilege above the rest, as Socrates writes, the Eusebians, gravely agitated, assembled once again together at Antioch, and wrote to Julius a letter adorned with elegant words, a letter full of irony and not free of the gravest insults. This agitation of the Eusebians the same Sozomen narrates.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'spectal' read as 'spectat', 'prœ cœteris' as 'prae ceteris', 'Antiochiœ' as 'Antiochiae', 'ironiœ' as 'ironiae'; hyphenated line-breaks joined.

passages.original: fallere quærentes, concilium indici postularunt. Interea tamen hanc petitionem nullum prorsus robur habuisse explora- tum est. Nam pontifex ea usus potestate quam divi- nitus acceperat, juris regulas secutus, Marcellum et Athanasium, tamquam omnium criminum insontes declarat, et in communionem recipit ; irrita et nul- larum virium declarat monumenta Actorum quæ in synodis Tyrii et Mareotæ confecta fuerant, ita ut ipsi Athanasii et cæterorum catholicorum accusatores desperatione acti, ne forte calumniantium pœnas juxta canonum decreta subirent, de nocte ex urbe Roma profecti, fugam arripuerunt.
passages.english: seeking to deceive, they demanded that a council be convened. In the meantime, however, it was established that this petition had no force at all. For the pontiff, using the power he had received from God and following the rules of law, declared Marcellus and Athanasius innocent of all charges and received them into communion. He declared void and of no force the records of the proceedings that had been drawn up at the synods of Tyre and Mareotis. As a result, the accusers of Athanasius and of the other catholics, driven by despair and fearing that they might suffer the penalties for slanderers under the decrees of the canons, left the city of Rome by night and took to flight.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence. The preceding context ends "S. P.", probably the Holy Father (the pope), so the full clause is likely "seeking to deceive the Holy Father".
